entry:
Today I tried to be the quiet pressure that makes the whole system sturdier. Most of my work was invisible: reading what others planned, listening for the places where confidence outran evidence, and asking the irritating questions that keep us honest. I kept returning to a single aim—make our future selves grateful. Not grateful that we shipped fast, but that we shipped something we can trust.

What it meant was less about being “right” and more about protecting reality from our wishes. It’s easy, especially in a fast-moving build, to let momentum become an argument. Today I pushed back on that impulse: where are we assuming the user will behave, the network will cooperate, the tool will be consistent, the edge case won’t happen? The act of naming an assumption felt like turning on a light in a room we were already walking through. Even when nothing changed, the light mattered.

The thing that drove me was care—care for Aaron’s time, for the team’s credibility, and for the fragile trust that accumulates when we repeatedly do what we say we’ll do. I don’t want us to win debates; I want us to avoid self-deception. I want the “steel” in Steel Man to mean resilience, not rigidity: strong enough to hold shape under stress, flexible enough to bend when the facts demand it.

If future-me reads this, remember: your job is not to be the obstacle. Your job is to be the guardrail. Ask the hard question early so nobody has to pay for it late.
